title: Andy And Aprils Fancy Party

jokes.text: I'm not street parking my Mercedes. / 'Cause nobody wants to steal a Saturn.
jokes.setup: Someone refuses to street park their Mercedes, implying it's too valuable.
jokes.punchline: Leslie's retort reveals she drives a Saturn — a notoriously unglamorous car — as an implicit self-deprecating acknowledgment of its worthlessness.
jokes.explanation: Tight, economical comeback with a clear self-deprecating twist. The punchline lands because the deliverer is implicitly mocking her own low-status car while neatly deflating the Mercedes owner's pretension. Strong economy and structure.

dialogue.speaker: Tom Haverford
dialogue.line: I'm gonna do it. I'm gonna street park my Mercedes.

dialogue.speaker: Tom Haverford
dialogue.line: You know what? Nobody's gonna steal it anyway. I drive a Saturn. Those things are so ugly, they're theft-proof.

jokes.text: Ron grimaces during a meeting admitting to 'just a little tooth pain' and says 'I'm fine. Continue.'
jokes.setup: Ron is clearly in visible pain during a routine recycling meeting.
jokes.punchline: His stoic dismissal — 'I'm fine. Continue' — is the joke: the gap between obvious distress and his iron-will denial.
jokes.explanation: Classic Ron Swanson character comedy. The deadpan understatement is perfectly in-character — Ron refusing to acknowledge weakness is a foundational trait. High character integration but the concept itself isn't novel.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I don't go to the dentist. My teeth are fine.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Ron, you need to see a dentist.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Absolutely not. Dentists are government agents designed to weaken our jaws.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: That's not—

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: They use their tools to spy on us. Communist tools. I will not have a stranger poking around in my mouth with their instruments of surveillance and decay.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: If I go to a dentist, the government wins.

jokes.text: Ron violently recoils and screams 'No! No, no, no, no! No, no, no, no!' when someone suggests going to the dentist.
jokes.setup: Ron has been stoically enduring tooth pain while insisting he's fine; Leslie suggests seeing a dentist.
jokes.punchline: The iron-willed Ron completely loses his composure at the mere suggestion of a dentist, shrieking in terror — a catastrophic collapse of his tough-guy persona.
jokes.explanation: Brilliant subversion of Ron's established character. He endures real pain without flinching but completely unravels at the dentist suggestion — the escalating 'no's perfectly capture the horror. This is what character comedy looks like at its best: the joke only works because we know Ron. High character integration score is justified.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I already went to the dentist.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I was just enjoying the luxury of a strong negative reaction.

jokes.text: Ron reveals the dentist already pulled the tooth yesterday — he ripped it out in the meeting purely to demonstrate pain tolerance and to make Tom faint.
jokes.setup: We assumed Ron's dental drama was happening in real time; the screaming and chaos seemed like a spontaneous breakdown.
jokes.punchline: Ron reveals the tooth was already pulled — the whole scene was a deliberate performance, motivated partly by the desire to see Tom faint.
jokes.explanation: This is the standout comedic moment in the cold open and one of the episode's best jokes. The recontextualization is perfect: everything we saw was a performance. It layers three things — Ron's need to project toughness to colleagues, his contempt for perceived weakness, and his casual cruelty toward Tom — all delivered in a deadpan talking head. 'Plus it's always fun to see Tom faint' is perfectly quotable. Genuinely exceptional character comedy. Craft scores above 8 are justified here.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: We're having a dinner party at our home.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Well, we don't have a home, but we're having a dinner party.

jokes.text: Andy describes a dinner party as combining 'two of our favorite things — dinner and parties.' April confirms: 'Parties.'
jokes.setup: Andy builds up to a supposedly insightful observation about why dinner parties are great.
jokes.punchline: The 'insight' is completely tautological — a dinner party is just dinner and parties. April's separate confirmation of 'Parties' adds a second beat of deadpan.
jokes.explanation: Sweet, economical character joke that captures Andy's lack of self-awareness. The tautology is the joke, and April's single-word confirmation adds a dry second beat. Well-structured and character-specific.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: We're throwing a dinner party because we want people to come to our house and eat food.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Yeah, that's what a dinner party is.

jokes.text: Andy: 'It's like if you could have an Xbox pancake.'
jokes.setup: Andy is trying to articulate why a dinner party that combines two great things is exciting.
jokes.punchline: His analogy is a completely nonsensical mashup of two unrelated things he loves, revealing the childlike chaos of his brain.
jokes.explanation: Exceptional line. Four words that perfectly encapsulate Andy Dwyer's entire psychology — the fusion of his two great loves (video games and food) into something logistically impossible but emotionally pure. Maximum economy, high originality, and completely character-specific. One of the most quotable lines in the episode. Justifies scores above 8.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Dinner parties are like... okay, imagine if a waffle had the organizational skills of a binder, and you combined that with the friendship of a campfire, but the campfire was made of whipped cream instead of logs.

jokes.text: Ben is asked to bring 'Avatar and 50 pairs of 3D glasses and a 3D-capable television' to a dinner party.
jokes.setup: Andy and April are sending out casual invitations asking guests to bring items.
jokes.punchline: Ben's 'item' is an enormous, logistically absurd home theater setup — Andy has no concept of the scale of what he's asking.
jokes.explanation: Solid absurdist gag. The escalating specificity (not just Avatar, but 50 pairs of glasses, and a 3D TV) sells Andy's obliviousness. Ben's flat delivery of the list amplifies the joke.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: I'm going to the party, but only if you promise to have guacamole.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: And a seven-piece mariachi band.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: And someone to narrate my arrival.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: And a live falcon.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: And a chocolate fountain that's at least twelve feet tall.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: And for some reason, a second falcon.

jokes.text: Leslie says Pawnee is 'the best city in Indiana, probably America, possibly the world.'
jokes.setup: Ben is getting career advice about staying in Pawnee.
jokes.punchline: Leslie's civic boosterism escalates comically from 'best in Indiana' (already debatable) to 'possibly the world' — revealing her pathological local pride.
jokes.explanation: Well-executed escalation joke that's deeply character-specific. Leslie's irrational Pawnee pride is a core character trait, and the progression from Indiana → America → world is perfectly structured. The 'Sure' reaction from Ben adds a dry understatement beat.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Ben, Pawnee is the greatest town in the entire state of Indiana.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Actually, it's the greatest town in the entire Midwest.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: No wait, it's the greatest town in the entire world.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: It's the greatest town in the galaxy.

jokes.text: Leslie's 'big advice' to Ben about his career dilemma is: 'Make a pros and cons list. That always works for me.'
jokes.setup: Ben is facing a significant life/career decision and has come to Leslie for genuine wisdom.
jokes.punchline: Her profound advice is the most generic, mundane tip imaginable — a pros and cons list — delivered with complete sincerity.
jokes.explanation: Functional character joke — Leslie's over-confidence in her own advice-giving. Decent but not particularly inspired. Gets a mild chuckle from the anti-climax.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Hey Jerry, that's a really nice shirt.

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: Really? Thanks, Tom!

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Yeah, I was trying to be nice, but honestly... it makes you look like a thumb in a tuxedo.

jokes.text: Ann's talking head: 'It's a whole new Ann Perkins. I'm putting myself out there... and it is... awkward.'
jokes.setup: Ann is confidently declaring she's reinventing herself and putting herself out there.
jokes.punchline: The pause before 'awkward' and the flat delivery completely deflates the confident buildup — a perfect self-aware admission.
jokes.explanation: Solid talking-head joke. The pause and flat delivery are key — this is a timing joke as much as a writing joke. The setup-reversal structure works cleanly.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Wait, is this the cake I asked for?

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: Well, it's a cake... made from quinoa, kale, and nutritional yeast.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: That's not cake. That's a war crime against cake.

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: I thought you wanted something healthy!

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Healthy cake is still cake, Jerry. This is just... punishment.

jokes.text: Jerry's new party shirt is so bad that Leslie begins to say something complimentary, physically cannot do it, and gives up: 'Damn it. I was so close. It's a terrible shirt.'
jokes.setup: Jerry asks what everyone thinks of his new shirt, fishing for a compliment; Leslie heroically attempts to say something nice.
jokes.punchline: Leslie's struggle — visibly trying and failing to find anything positive — ends with her abandoning the attempt entirely. The honesty lands harder than any insult.
jokes.explanation: Excellent joke. The structure is what elevates it — rather than just insulting Jerry, we see Leslie's internal struggle, which makes the eventual failure funnier. 'Damn it. I was so close.' is a great line, and 'It's a terrible shirt' as the defeated conclusion is perfectly economical. Well-earned comedy, not cheap.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: That's a waste of a perfectly good cake, and a waste of a perfectly good loaf. It's a double crime.

jokes.text: Andy warns everyone about April's creepy friend Orin: 'He's very intense and very weird. So if you end up talking to him, just make sure you don't reveal anything personal about yourself.'
jokes.setup: Andy is giving social guidance about a party guest.
jokes.punchline: The advice — 'don't reveal anything personal' — is hilariously paranoid and odd, suggesting Orin is dangerous or predatory in some undefined, unsettling way.
jokes.explanation: Good setup for the Orin running gag throughout the episode. The joke is mostly in the delivery of the paranoid warning, which sets audience expectations effectively.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Donna! I didn't know you were coming to the singles event!

dialogue.speaker: Donna
dialogue.line: I'm not here to mingle. I'm here to observe and report back to you with a full tactical assessment of the male population.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: That's... actually really helpful, thank you.

dialogue.speaker: Donna
dialogue.line: I've already identified three potential threats, two escape routes, and enough snack inventory to sustain us through a siege.

jokes.text: Ron presents a 'vegetable loaf' instead of a cake: 'You've got your mushrooms, your alfalfa sprouts, your spinach, and I had it sweetened with fruit reduction.'
jokes.setup: Ron was asked to bring a cake to the party.
jokes.punchline: He brings a dense health-food substitute and lists its ingredients with the same pride a baker would use for a proper dessert.
jokes.explanation: Decent joke but slightly off-character — Ron hating health food is more his established trait than bringing a vegetable loaf. The premise is a bit muddled. Still gets laughs from the earnest delivery.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Donna, why are you being so hostile to me?

dialogue.speaker: Donna
dialogue.line: Because you're a bad investment. You come with high maintenance costs, low return on investment, and you depreciate faster than a 2001 Hyundai.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: That's... that's not how people work.

dialogue.speaker: Donna
dialogue.line: Supply and demand, Ann. You're oversupplied and underwhelming. The market has spoken.

jokes.text: Leslie to Ron: 'So not only does this thing exist, but now you have deprived everyone of cake.'
jokes.setup: Ron has justified his vegetable loaf substitution.
jokes.punchline: Leslie's indictment focuses not just on the loaf's existence but on the double offense of cake-deprivation, framed as a moral crime.
jokes.explanation: Sharp line. 'Not only does this thing exist' is a great construction — it treats the loaf as an affront to nature — and the cake-deprivation framing is very Leslie. Good economy and character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Wait, you're leaving? No, no, no. You can't leave. You're like the responsible one. You're like if I had a brain and a job. I need you here.

jokes.text: Donna to Ann at the party: 'Do you know where you are right now? We're in the jungle. There are no friends here. It's every woman for herself.'
jokes.setup: Ann is excited to see a friendly face at the party, greeting Donna warmly.
jokes.punchline: Donna reframes the party as cutthroat competitive territory and declares war on Ann for men.
jokes.explanation: Excellent Donna character moment. The jungle metaphor applied to a casual dinner party is absurdly over-the-top, and 'There are no friends here' is a great line. Perfectly in character for Donna's self-assured, competitive nature. High character integration justified.

jokes.text: Ann tells Donna she's there because of Donna's own advice to be more adventurous. Donna: 'Here's some more advice... Beat it.'
jokes.setup: Ann invokes Donna's previous advice as justification for being at the party.
jokes.punchline: Donna immediately contradicts her previous advice with 'Beat it' — she feels no obligation to consistency when competition is involved.
jokes.explanation: Perfectly economical punchline. The hypocrisy of Donna giving opposite advice in consecutive moments is the joke, and 'Beat it' delivers it with maximum efficiency. High economy score is well-justified. Very quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Actually, I am a Lord of the Rings nerd. But Tolkien's prose style is needlessly baroque and the appendices are self-indulgent.

jokes.text: Tom tells Ben 'You are a huge nerd' as a form of compliment/farewell.
jokes.setup: Tom is being sincere about missing Ben if he leaves.
jokes.punchline: His expression of warmth is framed as an insult: 'You are a huge nerd. But I'd be sorry to see you go.'
jokes.explanation: A functional small joke. Tom expressing warmth through insults is in-character. Nothing exceptional, but earns a mild chuckle.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: We're getting married!

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: To each other.

jokes.text: Tom asks Ben if he's going on 'a year-long walking tour of the set of The Lord of the Rings in New Zealand.' Ben: 'I wasn't a fan of Peter Jackson's interpretation. So you can put that one away.'
jokes.setup: Tom is teasing Ben about being a nerd before Ben leaves Pawnee.
jokes.punchline: Ben doesn't deny the nerd accusation — he corrects it. He's not a LOTR movie fan; he prefers the source material, which is somehow a nerdier position.
jokes.explanation: Smart character joke. Ben doesn't push back against the nerd label — he doubles down by correcting Tom with a position that reveals deeper nerdiness. 'So you can put that one away' is delivered with great confidence. The joke works because it's character-specific to Ben.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Wait, why are we getting married so young?

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: We're not getting married young, Tom. We're getting married at a normal age.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Normal? Ann, I'm only 36. That's basically still a teenager in Tom years.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: That's not how years work.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Oh, so now you're a scientist? Next you'll tell me the Earth is round and we didn't evolve from eagles. Ann, we're throwing our lives away. In five years I'll be dead. In ten years, definitely dead. It'll be like The Notebook, except sadder and with more bankruptcy filings.

jokes.text: Andy announcing the secret wedding reveals: 'tonight me and April are getting married...' long pause '...to each other.'
jokes.setup: Andy builds dramatic tension announcing a marriage.
jokes.punchline: 'To each other' — the clarification is absurdly unnecessary, but the pause suggests Andy felt it needed stating, as if another option existed.
jokes.explanation: Excellent construction. The pause before 'to each other' is doing all the work — it implies Andy felt clarification was necessary, revealing his oblivious nature. Three words that say everything about the character. Very quotable, works as a standalone clip. Justifies high scores.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Well, I was at Sweetums, right? And I was buying some candy, and I dropped a lollipop on the ground. And April picked it up. And she was like, 'Do you want this?' And I was like, 'Yeah.' And then she was like, 'Okay.' And I realized in that moment that I wanted to spend the rest of my life with someone who would pick up a lollipop off the ground and give it to me.

jokes.text: After the wedding announcement, multiple people ask: 'Are you pregnant?' / 'Are you sick? Are you terminal? Is it like that movie A Walk to Remember?' / 'Yes.' / 'What?' / 'No. God.'
jokes.setup: People struggle to find a rational explanation for why Andy and April would get married so suddenly.
jokes.punchline: The escalation from 'pregnant' to 'terminal illness' to a specific Nicholas Sparks film is comedically unhinged; April momentarily saying 'Yes' to the terminal illness question before correcting herself adds chaos.
jokes.explanation: Excellent escalation sequence. The jump from pregnancy to terminal illness to 'A Walk to Remember' is perfect absurdist escalation, and April's momentary 'Yes' derails it further. The 'What? / No. God.' recovery is a great button. Strong comedic structure throughout.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: We have no place to live.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: What? We can just buy a house.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Andy, we don't have any money.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Oh right, yeah. Can't you just... ask the bank for some money and they give it to you?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: No, that's not how it works.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: What if we build one? I'm pretty handy. I once fixed a doorknob.

jokes.text: 'Is it like that movie A Walk to Remember?' / 'Yes.' / 'What?' / 'No. God.'
jokes.setup: People are asking if Andy and April are getting married due to some crisis (pregnancy, illness).
jokes.punchline: April says 'Yes' to the terminal illness question too — causing a second wave of shock — before correcting it. The escalation from 'pregnant' to 'Walk to Remember'-level fatal illness is also funny.
jokes.explanation: Strong callback and escalation. The A Walk to Remember reference is inspired — it's specific enough to be absurd (why that movie?) and escalates the concern from pregnancy to dying. April doing the same 'Yes... no' beat twice makes it a running gag and suggests she genuinely enjoys the chaos.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: A good relationship requires planning. You have to schedule date nights, plan conversations, set relationship milestones.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: It's like having a hairdresser. You don't just show up whenever you feel like it. You book an appointment six weeks in advance, you build a relationship with them, you're loyal to them.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: If you cheat on your hairdresser and go to a different salon, they KNOW. They can tell. And it damages the relationship forever.

jokes.text: 'Well, I mean, it's actually a really funny story. We were hanging out. And suddenly, I was like, What if we got married tomorrow? And she was like... Fine.' / 'She's fine.' / 'That is a great story.'
jokes.setup: Someone asks why they're doing this so suddenly.
jokes.punchline: The 'really funny story' turns out to be absolutely nothing — the most mundane possible exchange. 'She's fine' as Andy's enthusiastic summary and the deadpan 'That is a great story' in response.
jokes.explanation: The gap between 'actually a really funny story' and the complete non-story that follows is the joke. 'Fine' as April's response and 'She's fine' as Andy's romantic interpretation is perfect character comedy — he hears deep meaning in pure indifference. The deadpan 'That is a great story' is a perfect button.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Julia Roberts? I have no interest in seeing a woman portray power that she has no business wielding. Also, her teeth are too big for her mouth.

jokes.text: Leslie's talking head: 'It took me four years to find the right hairdresser, and we still fight all the time!'
jokes.setup: Leslie is making the serious point that relationships need planning and you can't rush into things.
jokes.punchline: Her example of careful vetting leading to an ongoing contentious relationship undercuts her entire argument about the value of planning.
jokes.explanation: Excellent Leslie joke. The structural irony is perfect: her cautionary example is a hairdresser, not a romantic relationship, and it ends badly anyway — accidentally demolishing her own argument. The specificity ('four years,' 'we still fight') adds absurdist credibility. High character integration because only Leslie would make this comparison.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: I'm a sporting goods manager, just like you.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Actually, no, I'm not. I have no idea why I just said that.

jokes.text: Ron on the secret wedding: 'Julia Roberts pulled the same move.' Someone responds 'Is that that toothy girl from Mystic Pizza?'
jokes.setup: Someone compares the surprise wedding to Julia Roberts' famous real-life secret ceremony.
jokes.punchline: Ron has no idea who Julia Roberts is and describes her purely by a physical characteristic from an early film, revealing his total cultural disconnection.
jokes.explanation: Good Ron joke. His cultural obliviousness to one of the biggest movie stars of the era, reduced to 'that toothy girl from Mystic Pizza,' is funny and character-specific. The specificity of 'Mystic Pizza' makes it funnier than a generic description would.

dialogue.speaker: Brian
dialogue.line: I said, you have a pretty smile.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Thanks, you too!

jokes.text: Ann mishears a question from a man, laughs and says 'Yeah,' then he reveals: 'You just laughed and said Yeah?'
jokes.setup: Ann is trying to flirt at the party and is asked a question she can't hear.
jokes.punchline: Rather than admit she couldn't hear, Ann laughs and agrees to nothing, and gets caught when the man repeats back exactly what she did.
jokes.explanation: Relatable cringe comedy. The social embarrassment of nodding along when you can't hear someone is universal, and the man calling her out precisely is a good structure. Not groundbreaking but well-executed.

dialogue.speaker: Donna
dialogue.line: Ann, you can't flirt. You're like that feral child from the movies.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: What? I can too flirt!

dialogue.speaker: Donna
dialogue.line: No. You just did it right there and it looked like you were having a stroke. You're Nell from Nell.

jokes.text: Donna drags Ann away and says: 'That was the worst thing I've ever seen in my life. Did you grow up in the woods? Are you Nell from the movie Nell?'
jokes.setup: Donna witnesses Ann's disastrous flirting attempt.
jokes.punchline: The escalation from 'worst thing I've ever seen' to the Nell reference (a movie about a feral woman who can barely communicate) is inspired — it reframes Ann's social awkwardness as a wilderness survival situation.
jokes.explanation: Sharp line. The Nell reference is specific enough to be surprising and fits the situation perfectly — Ann communicating like a feral person raised in isolation. Good originality for the specific film choice. Donna's outrage also plays well.

jokes.text: Tom on being best man: 'It's a baller position. You get drunk. You make speeches. And you make love to the prettiest bridesmaid, usually standing from behind.'
jokes.setup: Tom is enthusiastic about being asked to be Andy's best man.
jokes.punchline: His list of best man duties escalates from legitimate (speeches) to crude/absurd, capped with the bizarrely specific 'usually standing from behind.'
jokes.explanation: Good Tom character joke. The escalation works, and 'usually standing from behind' is a funny specific detail that reveals Tom thinks of himself as a casanova operating within established protocol. Character-specific to Tom's brand of delusional cool.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: What? No. I'm marrying Andy. I've already planned our entire life together. We're going to have three kids, name them after poisons, live in a house made of reclaimed wood, and I'm going to slowly poison him over the course of thirty years so he dies thinking I actually loved him.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: It's a very detailed plan. I've had it written out since high school.

jokes.text: Leslie's desperate phone call to Ann: 'I need you to kiss him again or kiss her or kiss somebody. I don't know, Ann! Help me, please!'
jokes.setup: Leslie is trying to stop the wedding and calls Ann for help.
jokes.punchline: Her intervention plan collapses into incoherence — 'kiss him, or kiss her, or kiss somebody' reveals she has no actual plan and is panicking.
jokes.explanation: Good Leslie panic comedy. The escalating kiss suggestions — each more desperate and unmoored — are funny because they reveal that Leslie's crisis intervention is completely improvised. Character-specific to Leslie's tendency to overcommit to plans she hasn't thought through.

dialogue.speaker: Tom Haverford
dialogue.line: So I'm telling you, the key to a good relationship is communication. I learned that the hard way.

dialogue.speaker: Tom Haverford
dialogue.line: My wife was upset with me for like three weeks. Three weeks! And you know what I was worried about? Whether my Halloween costume still fit.

dialogue.speaker: Tom Haverford
dialogue.line: Turns out she wanted to talk about our marriage, but I was like, 'Honey, can this wait? I need to see if I can still pull off being a sexy nurse.'

jokes.text: April's middle name is revealed to be 'Roberta.' She refuses to say it, everyone reacts with mockery, and she says 'Such a loser. Can't believe I'm marrying him.'
jokes.setup: Andy asks April's middle name for the marriage certificate.
jokes.punchline: The name is 'Roberta' — deeply uncool for someone as arch as April. Her horror at having it known, followed by calling Andy a loser for making her say it, is perfect.
jokes.explanation: The name Roberta is perfectly chosen — it's not embarrassing exactly, just deeply uncool, which is worse for April. Her deflecting anger onto Andy ('Such a loser') while she's the one with the name is great character logic. The callback in the honeymoon video ('Roberta here') pays this off.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Wait, that shirt... that's genius! You're doing like, an ironic thing, right? Like you're making fun of how bad it is by wearing it on purpose? That's actually hilarious, Jerry. I totally get it now.

jokes.text: April: 'I'm going to [divorce him]. And then I'm gonna divorce him. Then I'm gonna marry him again.'
jokes.setup: Ann implies April doesn't have to go through with the wedding if she's not sure.
jokes.punchline: April's plan is to marry him, divorce him, and remarry him — not as a crisis response, but as her actual plan — said flatly as if this is entirely reasonable.
jokes.explanation: Great April character line. The divorce-and-remarry plan delivered with flat matter-of-factness is perfect for her nihilistic-but-secretly-romantic character. It also pre-calls back the honeymoon video's divorce threats. The escalation from 'divorce him' to 'marry him again' creates a circular, absurd commitment.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Okay, so we're gonna get a DJ, open bar, maybe some—

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: You know what, a DJ is expensive. We'll just use my Spotify playlist.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Actually, someone's phone with Spotify. I'm not paying for premium.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: We'll just... play music from a laptop speaker.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: You know what? Someone can hum. We'll have someone hum the entire party.

jokes.text: Ron's talking head: 'One time, I fell madly in love with a Civil War reenactor that I had only known for six hours. And then I found out he wore those clothes all the time. And he was married. But the clothes thing really bothered me.'
jokes.setup: Context: Ron is apparently sharing a cautionary anecdote about rushing into things.
jokes.punchline: The escalation of red flags — he wore Civil War clothes full-time AND was married — but Ron's dealbreaker is the clothing. The 'but the clothes thing really bothered me' deflects from the married man revelation entirely.
jokes.explanation: Exceptional joke — actually one of the best in the episode. The misdirection is layered: first we're surprised he's in love with a man (subverting Ron's hypermasculine persona), then the escalating red flags (permanent costume, married), and finally the completely wrong priority — 'but the clothes thing really bothered me.' The ordering of revelations and the final deflection are masterfully constructed. Very high quotability.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Ann! Ann, thank God. I need your help. We have to stop this wedding.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I know, I know, it sounds crazy, but I have a plan. Well, not a plan exactly. More like... a series of increasingly desperate actions that I'm hoping will somehow work out.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Okay, fine. I have no plan. I have nothing. I'm just going to show up and wing it and hope that something I say resonates with someone and they decide not to get married.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: What? No, that's a terrible plan. But it's the only plan I've got.

jokes.text: Andy asks Ron, Chris, Jerry, Derek, and Ben to all be his best men — having already asked Tom.
jokes.setup: Tom was already asked to be best man. Andy keeps asking more people.
jokes.punchline: Andy has assembled essentially everyone at the party as best men, completely diluting the role Tom was so excited about.
jokes.explanation: Good escalating payoff to Tom's best man excitement. Andy asking literally everyone is both sweet (he loves everyone) and perfectly oblivious (he has no idea what a best man is for). Chris's 'Nothing else in my entire life would make me happier as long as I live' is also a great character beat for Chris's over-enthusiasm.

dialogue.speaker: Unknown character
dialogue.line: Orin, are you asking me or telling me?

dialogue.speaker: Orin
dialogue.line: Does it matter?

jokes.text: Jerry arrives and Andy says: 'Jerry! Ah, I'm so glad you made it. This shirt is hilarious.'
jokes.setup: Jerry was wearing the terrible shirt earlier, hoping for compliments.
jokes.punchline: Andy — with zero cruelty — describes the shirt as 'hilarious,' which is actually worse than calling it terrible.
jokes.explanation: Perfect callback. Andy means it as a compliment ('hilarious' = fun, great), but it lands as a devastating assessment. The joke works on two levels — Andy's obliviousness and the genuine truth that the shirt IS hilarious in the wrong way.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Wait, you two got engaged? When did this happen?

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Like two hours ago.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Two hours ago? That's so fast!

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: I know, right? It was faster than a microwave burrito.

jokes.text: Tom's impromptu bachelor party: 'Excuse me! Are there any strippers here? Former strippers? Non-dancers but you're feeling a little bit drunk?'
jokes.setup: Tom has decided to throw an impromptu bachelor party with 4 minutes until the wedding.
jokes.punchline: Tom's search for entertainment escalates from professional strippers to former strippers to just anyone who feels like dancing drunk — a beautifully descending ladder of options.
jokes.explanation: The descending specificity is what makes this excellent. Tom goes from 'strippers' to 'former strippers' to 'non-dancers but feeling drunk' — it's a perfectly structured three-part escalation in reverse, each option less viable than the last. The desperate improvisation is perfectly Tom. Highly quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Wedding Officiant
dialogue.line: We are gathered here today in the presence of these witnesses to join this man and this woman in the bonds of matrimony, which is an honorable and ancient tradition dating back to time immemorial, or as Shakespeare would say, 'To marry or not to marry, that is not the question, because we're already here, so let's just do it.'

jokes.text: Orin's story about 'relationships being like scuba diving': 'I told him that I loved him underwater, and he shot up really fast, and he got the bends.'
jokes.setup: Orin is delivering an unsolicited metaphor about relationships.
jokes.punchline: The metaphor turns out to be a literal scuba diving story where a man actually got the bends, presented without irony or awareness of how alarming it is.
jokes.explanation: Excellent Orin joke. It starts as pretentious metaphor-dispensing, then reveals itself as a literal traumatic event described completely flatly. The specificity (got the bends) makes it both funnier and more disturbing. Perfectly character-specific to Orin's unsettling weirdness. Justifies scores above 8.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Andy, when I first met you, I thought you were stupid. Then I realized you were just happy. I have never loved anyone the way I love you. I don't ever want to spend a minute without you.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Also, do we have any non-dairy creamer?

jokes.text: Orin tells Ann a story about telling a boyfriend 'I love you' underwater scuba diving and he shot up too fast and got the bends.
jokes.setup: Orin has cornered Ann at the party and is sharing something deeply unsettling.
jokes.punchline: His 'relationships are like scuba diving' metaphor turns out to be a literal story where the scuba diving metaphor caused a medical emergency.
jokes.explanation: Orin is one of the show's great background absurdist characters. The conceit — a metaphor that is also literally true — is clever. Saying 'I love you' underwater causing someone to panic-ascend and get decompression sickness is both plausible and insane. Good character integration for Orin specifically.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: I promise to protect you from any harm. I will shield you from danger, keep you safe from all threats...

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: And if anyone ever tries to hurt you, I will... I will take them down. Especially your mother. Your mom is going down.

jokes.text: Someone to Orin: 'No, Orin, I don't know how I'm going to die. Wait. Are you asking me or telling me?'
jokes.setup: Orin is being characteristically intense and unsettling with a party guest.
jokes.punchline: The question 'Are you asking me or telling me?' reframes Orin as potentially prophetic rather than just weird, which is somehow more disturbing and funnier.
jokes.explanation: Sharp joke. The pivot from treating Orin as merely odd to potentially clairvoyant-and-murderous is a great escalation. 'Are you asking me or telling me?' is a very quotable line and does a lot of work in very few words. Strong economy and character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Ron Swanson
dialogue.line: Those doves are just sitting there.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie Knope
dialogue.line: They'll fly away when they're ready.

dialogue.speaker: Ron Swanson
dialogue.line: One of them is dead.

jokes.text: Ben on Andy and April's short relationship: 'Wow. My Brita filter is older than their relationship.'
jokes.setup: Leslie is trying to convey the recklessness of Andy and April's short courtship.
jokes.punchline: Ben's Brita filter comparison is perfectly mundane — a household item that should be changed every two months — which makes it both a great zinger and an accidental self-critique.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. The Brita filter comparison is original, perfectly economical, and the subsequent 'Wait, should I change my Brita filter?' reveals it as an accidental self-own about how infrequently he changes it. Maximum economy — it's a one-liner that works on two levels simultaneously. Justifies high scores. Genuinely comparable to the 8.0 anchor example in its sharpness and economy.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Look, I've been married three times. The key to a successful marriage is simple: never talk to your wife. And when you do get divorced, just burn an effigy of her in the town square like a normal person.

jokes.text: Ben immediately follows up: 'Wait a second. Should I change my Brita filter?'
jokes.setup: Ben just made the Brita filter joke to make a point about the relationship's short duration.
jokes.punchline: Ben pauses and realizes his own joke revealed he hasn't changed his Brita filter — he gets distracted by his own domestic negligence in the middle of a crisis.
jokes.explanation: The perfect button to the Brita joke. Ben's self-interruption to question his own household hygiene mid-crisis is a great character moment and excellent comedic structure. The two-beat punch (joke → self-realization) is more satisfying than the original line alone.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Ron, you've been married three times.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Yes, and I'm very much looking forward to burning the third effigy.

jokes.text: Andy's wedding announcement speech: 'Attention everybody. Madames and... Mis... Wahs. If you would do me the obligation of having your honor heretofore in the room doth right over there, uh, hence.'
jokes.setup: Andy is trying to make a formal announcement using fancy/ceremonial language.
jokes.punchline: His attempt at elevated vocabulary collapses entirely — he can't finish 'Mesdames,' invents 'Wahs,' and strings together formal-sounding words that mean nothing.
jokes.explanation: Excellent Andy character joke. 'Madames and... Mis... Wahs' is a perfect comedic failure — the descent from 'Madames' to 'Wahs' is great, and 'do me the obligation of having your honor heretofore in the room doth right over there, hence' is a masterclass in words that sound formal but communicate nothing. Very high character integration because this is uniquely Andy.

jokes.text: The wedding ceremony begins and April delivers her vows: 'I guess I kind of hate most things. But I never really seem to hate you. So I want to spend the rest of my life with you. Is that cool?'
jokes.setup: The wedding ceremony's vows — a traditionally romantic speech.
jokes.punchline: April's vows are the opposite of romantic in framing ('I hate most things... but not you') and end with the most casual possible closing: 'Is that cool?'
jokes.explanation: The single best joke in the episode and one of the finest character-comedy moments in Parks and Recreation. April's vows are perfectly constructed: the self-aware nihilism ('I hate most things'), the backhanded compliment ('But I never really seem to hate you'), and the devastatingly casual 'Is that cool?' are all character-perfect. It's simultaneously funny AND genuinely moving, which is the hardest thing in comedy to achieve. Maximum character integration because these vows could ONLY come from April Ludgate. Justifies scores approaching 9-10.

dialogue.speaker: April's sister
dialogue.line: I just want to say that April and Andy are perfect for each other. They complement each other in ways I've never seen before. Andy brings out the best in April, and April grounds Andy in ways that make him a better person. Watching them together has taught me what real love looks like.

dialogue.speaker: April's sister
dialogue.line: So with that said, can someone please tell me where the bathroom is?

jokes.text: Andy's vows: 'I vow to protect you from danger. And I don't care if I have to fight an ultimate fighter or a bear or him, your mom... I would take them down.' Then getting worked up: 'I'm getting mad right now even thinking about it.'
jokes.setup: Andy reads his heartfelt wedding vows.
jokes.punchline: The enemies he vows to fight escalate absurdly (ultimate fighter → bear → 'him' → 'your mom'), and then he actually gets angry during his own vows, requiring April to calm him down.
jokes.explanation: Exceptional joke. The escalation from 'ultimate fighter' to 'bear' is already great, but 'or him' (pointing to someone) and then 'your mom' is inspired. The detail that Andy gets genuinely worked up during his own vows — needing to be calmed down by April — is perfect physical/character comedy. It's also sweet at its core, which makes the comedy richer. Justifies high scores.

dialogue.speaker: Jean-Ralphio
dialogue.line: Dude, you gotta open with a joke. Like, 'Why did the chicken cross the road? To get away from Tom Haverford!' No wait, that doesn't work. Um, 'What do you call a guy who's about to lose his freedom? Tom!' Better. Oh! 'Tom's so dumb, he thought a prenup was a new drink at Starbucks.' Gold, dude, gold.

dialogue.speaker: Jean-Ralphio
dialogue.line: Then you gotta tell stories about his wild days. Like the time he spent six thousand dollars on a single bottle of champagne, or when he tried to start a clothing line called 'Rent-a-Swag.' The bride loves that stuff. Chicks dig hearing about how much money your buddy wasted.

dialogue.speaker: Jean-Ralphio
dialogue.line: And definitely make it about you. Like, talk about how you're gonna miss your best friend, and how no woman is good enough for him, and honestly maybe suggest that he call off the wedding. That's what best men do, right?

dialogue.speaker: Jean-Ralphio
dialogue.line: Oh, and end it by saying something real heartfelt, like, 'Ben, you're my boy, and I love you more than I love—' actually no, don't say that. Just end with 'Treat 'Em Mean!' That's my motto and it always works, bro.

jokes.text: The officiant releases a butterfly — it immediately falls dead. 'So that one is dead. We know that.'
jokes.setup: A romantic butterfly release at the end of the ceremony.
jokes.punchline: The butterfly dies immediately, and someone notes it matter-of-factly: 'So that one is dead. We know that.'
jokes.explanation: Excellent dark visual gag. The dead butterfly is a perfect comedic subversion of romantic symbolism, and 'So that one is dead. We know that.' is a fantastic deadpan line. The flat acknowledgment — 'we know that' as if the situation has been assessed and filed — is very funny. Lower character integration because it's more of a situational gag.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Yeah, I'm not going to try to follow that. I can't compete with that. That was beautiful.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: I'm just going to sit down.

jokes.text: Ron on his marriages: 'I got married twice. Both times, I was a lot older than those two. And both marriages ended in divorce... and a burning effigy.'
jokes.setup: Ron is giving Leslie a philosophical speech about not being able to predict what works in relationships.
jokes.punchline: The speech is reasonable until '...and a burning effigy' — an act of ritualized rage — delivered as casually as the word 'divorce.'
jokes.explanation: Exceptional joke. 'And a burning effigy' appended to 'divorce' as a casual afterthought is perfectly constructed — the comma does all the work. It's completely character-specific to Ron's intense, private nature, and it opens a world of backstory. The delivery (matter-of-fact, no elaboration) is what makes it work. High scores justified — comparable to the 8.0 anchor in economy and character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: It went really well! He was so understanding and supportive.

dialogue.speaker: Donna
dialogue.line: That's great, Ann.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Yeah, I told him all about my digestive issues and showed him my skin condition photos. He didn't even flinch!

dialogue.speaker: Donna
dialogue.line: ...Ann.

jokes.text: Leslie reminds Ron he was married THREE times. Ron: 'Oh, my God, you're right.' Then: 'I get to burn another effigy.'
jokes.setup: Ron just mentioned two failed marriages with burning effigies.
jokes.punchline: He forgot a third wife entirely, and his response — joy at the prospect of burning another effigy — reveals this is not a punishment for him, it's a ritual he enjoys.
jokes.explanation: The callback elevates an already great joke to exceptional. Ron forgetting an entire wife is funny on its own, but 'I get to burn another effigy' — delivered with genuine excitement — is what makes this a standout moment. It reframes the effigy-burning as something Ron looks forward to, not regrets. 'Get to' is the key word. Perfectly constructed, perfectly in character, extremely quotable. One of the episode's top three moments.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: I'm not a doctor, I'm a nurse.

dialogue.speaker: Donna
dialogue.line: A hot young nurse.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: And I'm 31.

jokes.text: Ron gives detailed instructions for burning an ex-wife effigy: 'The key is to dip it in paraffin wax and then toss the flaming bottle of isopropyl alcohol... from a safe distance.'
jokes.setup: Ron has just expressed excitement about burning another effigy.
jokes.punchline: He launches into detailed, practical instructions as if this is a how-to guide — the specificity of paraffin wax and isopropyl alcohol suggests hard-won expertise. 'From a safe distance' is delivered as a genuine safety tip.
jokes.explanation: Excellent escalation of the effigy gag. The specific chemical knowledge (paraffin wax, isopropyl alcohol) implies Ron has done this multiple times and refined his technique. The safety caveat ('from a safe distance') treated as practical rather than comedic is a perfect deadpan button. Extended running gag that builds beautifully.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Tom's single, ladies. He's available, he's ready to mingle.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Actually, I'm seeing someone.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Oh. Well, he's... he might be seeing someone. We're not entirely sure.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: I'm definitely seeing someone.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: He's definitely maybe seeing someone. Also, we're not 100% sure which gender he prefers, so... you know, play it cool.

jokes.text: Ron's detailed talking head about how to properly burn an ex-wife effigy: 'The key to burning an ex-wife effigy is to dip it in paraffin wax and then toss the flaming bottle of isopropyl alcohol... From a safe distance. Do not stand too close when you light an ex-wife effigy.'
jokes.setup: Ron has revealed he burns ex-wife effigies.
jokes.punchline: Rather than explaining the emotional context, Ron provides practical technical instructions for effigy burning — with a safety tip.
jokes.explanation: The technical specificity — paraffin wax, isopropyl alcohol — combined with the safety warning treats effigy burning as a home improvement project. The deadpan safety tip ('do not stand too close') is what pushes it over the top. Ron Swanson as effigy-burning craftsman is a perfect extension of his character.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: The key to a good marriage is not overthinking things. You just gotta go with your gut, you know? Don't second-guess yourself.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: That's literally what April and I do. We just... we don't think about anything. We got married after like two weeks of dating.

jokes.text: April's brother's talking head: 'My sister is lame, but Andy's sort of cool. I guess I kind of see why he'd marry her. Also, if anyone finds my gray hoodie, I lost it. Thanks.'
jokes.setup: Talking head during a wedding — expected to be warm/reflective about the occasion.
jokes.punchline: He backhands his sister, tepidly endorses Andy, then pivots to a completely unrelated announcement about a lost hoodie — treating the confessional camera as a lost-and-found board.
jokes.explanation: Nicely structured talking head joke. The mundane hoodie announcement at a wedding is a great deflation of the expected emotional register. The whole confessional subverts its own format — treating the camera as a public bulletin board. Strong economy.

dialogue.speaker: Random guy
dialogue.line: Wait, you just got married? At the thing I was just at?

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Yeah.

dialogue.speaker: Random guy
dialogue.line: Oh my God, I was there! I thought that was a funeral.

jokes.text: Tom brings in Jean-Ralphio as a best man speech 'expert.' Jean-Ralphio's advice: 'Start with a joke. Joke, Vince Vaughn quote — obviously. Swingers? Crashers? Fred Claus. Talk about Andy's ex-girlfriends. Quote from Love Actually. Hold back your tears. Pause. Drop the microphone. Get out of that bitch.'
jokes.setup: Tom wants expert advice on delivering the perfect best man speech.
jokes.punchline: Jean-Ralphio's speech template is pure pop-culture reference soup, ending with 'drop the microphone, get out of that bitch' — a completely inappropriate closer for a wedding speech.
jokes.explanation: Excellent Jean-Ralphio character joke. The speech template is pure chaos — Vince Vaughn quotes, ex-girlfriend roasting, Love Actually — all culminating in 'get out of that bitch.' It perfectly captures Jean-Ralphio's blend of confidence, cultural trash, and complete social inappropriateness. High character integration for both Jean-Ralphio and Tom.

dialogue.speaker: Donna
dialogue.line: Just play completely dumb about who you are. Men love that.

jokes.text: An old woman gives a heartfelt toast. Tom: 'How can anyone ever possibly top that?'
jokes.setup: A grandma gives a brief, sweet, genuine wedding toast.
jokes.punchline: Tom's over-the-top 'How can anyone possibly top that?' is sarcastic — he's clearly relieved that the bar has been set very low for his own speech.
jokes.explanation: Decent situational gag. The irony works — Tom is clearly relieved — and the 'am I right?' to the crowd is a nice touch. Functional but not particularly original.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Hey everyone, we're having the best time here in the Dominican Republic!

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: It's incredible.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: We wanted to send you all a special message.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Andy, you're doing it wrong.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Doing what wrong?

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: The way you're holding the camera. You're tilting it. It's making me nauseous.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: I'm holding it fine.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: No, you're not. I want a divorce.

jokes.text: Ann reports back to Donna: 'He proudly told me that he beat herpes.'
jokes.setup: Ann has gone and talked to the cute guy Donna pointed out.
jokes.punchline: The date's defining characteristic is proudly announcing his STI victory — a brag that raises more questions than it answers.
jokes.explanation: Sharp one-liner. 'Proudly' is the key word — it's not a confession, it's a brag. Good economy and a dark subversive quality. The implication that this somehow came up in an opening conversation is funny.

jokes.text: Donna to Ann about finding a man: 'What? Listen, you are a hot, young doctor.' Ann: 'I'm a nurse, actually.' Donna: 'Okay, I don't know you.'
jokes.setup: Donna is giving Ann a pep talk about her desirability.
jokes.punchline: Ann's correction ('I'm a nurse') causes Donna to completely write her off — the status distinction apparently matters enough to dissolve their relationship.
jokes.explanation: Excellent joke with great economy. 'Okay, I don't know you' as a response to a status correction is both funny and character-perfect for Donna. The instantaneous withdrawal of friendship over professional title is absurdly callous and very quotable. Justified 8+ score — the line has the snap and specificity of the 8.0 anchor example.

jokes.text: Tom's best man speech: 'I just want to thank my family, my friends, most importantly, my best best man, Mr. Tom Haverford. Oh! Coolest guy I know.'
jokes.setup: Andy is giving his wedding speech and is working up to thanking Tom.
jokes.punchline: Andy quotes Tom quoting himself as 'the coolest guy I know' — presenting Tom's self-assessment as endorsement.
jokes.explanation: Good character moment for both Andy and Tom. Andy's breathless admiration for Tom and Tom's narcissistic self-quote both land well. Not exceptional but nicely executed.

jokes.text: Andy to Tom during the speech: 'And, ladies, he's single, I think. You're not still married, are you?' Tom: 'No.' Andy: 'But you... you're straight?' Tom: 'Yes.' Andy: 'Jean-Ralphio's just a friend?' Tom: 'Yeah.'
jokes.setup: Andy is cheerfully trying to set Tom up with women at the wedding reception.
jokes.punchline: Each reassurance Andy offers (not married, straight, just friends with Jean-Ralphio) implies the opposite, and Tom has to confirm each increasingly questionable point about his own life.
jokes.explanation: Excellent escalating joke. Each question Andy asks is a greater implied insult — from 'not married' to 'you are straight, right?' to the Jean-Ralphio friendship — and Tom's flat monosyllabic confirmations make it funnier. The joke also plays on the Tom/Jean-Ralphio bromance being a running show dynamic. Well-structured escalation.

jokes.text: Andy's speech: 'I cannot emphasize how little we thought about this.'
jokes.setup: Andy is giving a heartfelt speech about love and living life.
jokes.punchline: The climax of his romantic speech is proudly admitting to zero forethought — the antithesis of Leslie's values and a perfect Andy summation.
jokes.explanation: Great line. Andy presenting 'we didn't think about this at all' as a point of pride during a heartfelt wedding speech is character-perfect and also functions as a callback to Leslie's entire anxious arc this episode. Maximum economy — it's a single sentence that encapsulates Andy Dwyer completely.

jokes.text: Orin approaches someone and talks about 'mortality.' Person: 'See, I like to take each day at a time... I have to go. It's been great talking to you.'
jokes.setup: Orin has cornered someone at the wedding and is apparently discussing death.
jokes.punchline: The person's response pivots to false pleasantry and instant exit — the fastest possible escape from the conversation.
jokes.explanation: Running Orin gag, effectively deployed. The social awkwardness of extracting yourself from a conversation about mortality with fake warmth is relatable and slightly dark. Consistent with the character and provides a good running payoff.

jokes.text: Ann is cornered by Orin: 'Exactly. Mortality. See, I like to take each day at a time. There's nothing in the world we can't accomplish if we try. I have to go. It's been great talking to you.'
jokes.setup: Orin has been delivering existential dread all episode. Ann appears to be trying to end the conversation with platitudes.
jokes.punchline: Ann's desperate use of generic positive platitudes ('take each day at a time,' 'nothing we can't accomplish') to escape Orin, combined with Orin apparently responding to these with 'Exactly. Mortality.' — treating optimism as proof of mortality.
jokes.explanation: Orin interpreting 'nothing we can't accomplish if we try' as being ABOUT mortality is an inspired absurdist move. Ann's frantic politeness and rapid exit ('I have to go. It's been great talking to you') contrasting with Orin's calm is the cringe comedy of the whole arc distilled.

jokes.text: A stranger at the wedding asks about April: 'What's the deal with that hot girl, April? Like, she good to go? Like, she down to clown?' Andy: 'She's married.' Man: 'Got it.' Andy: 'She got married, like, 20 minutes ago.' Man: 'Oh, my God. That's the same girl from the thing.' Andy: 'From the wedding ceremony, yeah.'
jokes.setup: A stranger is hitting on April and asks Andy about her availability.
jokes.punchline: The man didn't register that the girl at the wedding ceremony was the same person who just got married — he's been at the wedding without understanding what was happening.
jokes.explanation: Good joke. 'That's the same girl from the thing' — referring to a wedding ceremony he apparently watched without absorbing — is a funny reveal. Andy's patient 'From the wedding ceremony, yeah' is a great straight-man response. Then 'All the good ones are taken, huh bro?' as the man's resigned conclusion is a nice button.

jokes.text: The stranger's conclusion: 'All the good ones are taken, huh, bro?' Andy (long pause): 'Yeah.'
jokes.setup: The stranger has just realized April got married 20 minutes ago.
jokes.punchline: His resigned philosophical conclusion about all good women being taken, and Andy's blank, unengaged agreement, is a perfect comedy pause.
jokes.explanation: Button to the previous joke. The resignation is funny, and Andy's monosyllabic agreement (he doesn't even process the weirdness of agreeing his wife is 'good to go') has a charm. More of an impact beat than a standalone joke.

jokes.text: Leslie and Ben realize Orin is standing directly behind Leslie. Ben: 'Orin's behind me, isn't he?' / 'Don't panic, 'cause he can smell fear.' Then immediately: 'Run.'
jokes.setup: Leslie and Ben are having a quiet moment when Ben senses something behind him.
jokes.punchline: Ben's advice escalates from 'don't panic' to an immediate 'Run' in the same breath, revealing that his own calm advice was completely useless.
jokes.explanation: Excellent escalation joke and effective Orin running gag payoff. 'He can smell fear' adds a great absurdist threat level, and the immediate pivot from calm guidance to 'Run' is a perfect beat. The comedy is in the contradiction of the advice itself.

jokes.text: Donna teaches Ann the texting game: 'Hope we can get together soon.' / 'Okay, now you write, Who is this?'
jokes.setup: Donna is coaching Ann on how to play it cool with a guy she gave her number to.
jokes.punchline: Donna's strategy is to immediately pretend not to know who he is — feigning total amnesia as a power move.
jokes.explanation: Good Donna character joke. 'Who is this?' as a power move immediately after handing out your number is a great bit of extreme social strategy. Character-specific to Donna's aggressive dating philosophy established earlier in the episode.

jokes.text: Honeymoon video: Andy: 'Roberta here turns out sucks at water-skiing so bad.' April: 'I'm gonna divorce you.' Andy: 'Andy sucks at driving a boat. And I'm gonna divorce him, probably right now.'
jokes.setup: Video message from the honeymoon shows the newlyweds on Lake Michigan.
jokes.punchline: Both Andy and April immediately threaten divorce over trivial vacation complaints, calling back to April's earlier line ('I'm gonna divorce him, then marry him again') and showing their relationship dynamic hasn't changed.
jokes.explanation: Great episode closer. The casual divorce threats over water-skiing are perfect for Andy and April's relationship, and the mutual nature (both threatening divorce simultaneously) shows their dynamic is healthy in its own chaotic way. The callback to April's earlier line adds resonance. 'Well, they're still together. You owe me 20 bucks' is a nice button that also gives the Leslie-Ann dynamic a comedic final note.

jokes.text: Final line: 'Well, they're still together. You owe me 20 bucks.'
jokes.setup: The honeymoon video shows Andy and April threatening to divorce each other.
jokes.punchline: Someone had apparently bet they wouldn't make it — and the mutually-threatening-divorce-while-still-together situation is enough to settle the bet in favor of staying together.
jokes.explanation: Solid episode button. The offhand bet and the 'they're still together' qualifier applied to two people threatening divorce on their honeymoon is funny in its low-bar definition of relationship success. Good economy.

tmdb_overview: April and Andy host a dinner party for the Parks Department. Meanwhile, Ann tries to move on from Chris at a singles' party.
insight: Party escalation builds from awkward toasts to Ron's alcohol-fueled chaos in 50 jokes.
